levels.intro: In this room: a fake delivery text, a phishing email, and two real emails that are safe.
levels.briefing:
You just joined the Cybercrime Investigation Unit. Your job: catch fake texts, emails and posts before they steal money, passwords or personal details.

This is your training case. A guide will walk you through your first question.
objectives: Follow the guide on your first question.
Score {unlock}+ to unlock the next room.

You reserved a book at Riverside Public Library on Monday.

lessons: Spot a fake delivery text: unexpected, rushed, a small fee and a strange link.
Name phishing and spot a fake look-alike address.
Recognise a real notice: it matches something you did, gives you time and asks for nothing secret.
Know that not every message is a scam: a real one from someone you know just shares details.

questions.message: SwiftParcel: Your package is ON HOLD due to an incomplete address. Pay the ₱29 redelivery fee within 12 hours or it will be returned:
questions.scenarioContext: You have not ordered anything this month.
questions.explanation: You didn't order anything, so there is no package. The text comes from a random mobile number, rushes you with a 12-hour deadline, and links to a site that isn't the courier's. The small fee is bait to get your card or e-wallet details.
questions.feedback: Scam! No order + a small fee + a rush deadline = a fake delivery text. Don't tap the link.
questions.hint: Compare the text with your case notes: were you expecting a package? Then check who sent it and where the link goes.
questions.learningObjective: Spot a fake delivery text: unexpected, rushed, a small fee and a strange link.
questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 16: Information Security Best Practices (user awareness)

clues.label: The request
clues.finding: A small fee is bait: the real goal is your card or e-wallet details.

clues.label: Deadline
clues.finding: A short deadline pushes you to act before you think.

clues.label: Link

questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.message: Email from: Campus IT Helpdesk <helpdesk@uphs1-binan.example> Subject: Mailbox 98% full: verify now "Your school mailbox will be DELETED in 24 hours. Click below and sign in to verify your account." What kind of threat is this?
choices: Phishing
Ransomware
Denial-of-service attack
A normal storage warning
questions.explanation: Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into giving away your password. This one copies the school (uphs1 uses the number 1, not the letter l), scares you with a deadline and asks you to sign in. Real storage warnings never ask for your password.
questions.feedback: Phishing! Look closely: uphs1, not uphsl. Fake sender + scary deadline + "sign in here" = phishing.
questions.hint: Check the sender's address letter by letter, then ask yourself what the email wants you to do.
questions.learningObjective: Name phishing and spot a fake look-alike address.
questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Introduction to Computer Security: "types of security threats… in both personal and organizational contexts"

clues.label: Sender address
clues.finding: Look closely: uphs1 uses the number 1 instead of the letter l. It's a lookalike of the school's real domain.

clues.label: Subject
clues.finding: Full mailboxes really happen. On its own this isn't a warning sign - look at what the email asks you to do.

clues.label: Threat
clues.finding: A scary deadline pushes you to act fast without checking.

clues.match: sign in to verify your account
clues.label: What it asks
clues.finding: It wants your password through a link. Real IT staff never ask you to 'verify' your password by email.

clues.label: The button
clues.finding: It leads to a sign-in page from an email link - the way fake pages collect passwords. (Simulated: nothing opens.)

indicators.title: Lookalike sender domain
indicators.whyItMatters: uphs1 is not uphsl - a fake address made to look real.

indicators.title: Scary deadline
indicators.whyItMatters: Threats and short deadlines are pressure tactics.

indicators.title: Asks you to sign in through a link
indicators.whyItMatters: That's how fake pages collect passwords.

questions.message: The book you reserved is now available at the front desk. It will be held for 7 days. Log in to your library account if you need more time.

questions.feedback: Legitimate! It matches what you did, there's no rush, and it asks for nothing secret.
questions.hint: Check your case notes: did you do something that explains this email? Then look at what it asks you to do.
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a real notice: it matches something you did, gives you time and asks for nothing secret.
questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 16: Information Security Best Practices (user awareness)

clues.label: Sender address
clues.finding: The address ends in the library's own name: riversidelibrary.example.

clues.match: The book you reserved is now available

clues.label: What it asks

clues.match: Log in to your library account

indicators.title: You were expecting it

indicators.title: Asks for nothing secret
indicators.whyItMatters: No link, money, password or code is requested.

indicators.title: No pressure

questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.message: A raffle booth at the mall asks you to fill in a form to join. Which of these is the biggest privacy warning sign?
choices: They want a photo of your ID and your birthdate just to join, with no notice saying why
The raffle is free to join
The staff wear company shirts
The draw is next week
questions.explanation: A raffle only needs a way to contact you, not your ID and birthdate. Together, those can be used to pretend to be you. The Data Privacy Act says they must explain why they collect data and take only what they need.
questions.feedback: Too much! An ID photo for a raffle? Ask why they need it and look for a privacy notice.
questions.hint: Think about what a raffle really needs from you just to contact a winner.
questions.learningObjective: Share personal data only when it's really needed and the reason is explained.
questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105) — Week 15: Data Privacy Act (RA 10173)

clues.label: Full name
clues.finding: A raffle needs to know who won. Asking for a name is reasonable.

clues.label: Mobile number
clues.finding: A raffle needs a way to contact the winner. This is proportionate.

clues.label: Birthdate
clues.finding: A raffle doesn't need your birthdate. Together with an ID photo it can be used for identity theft.

clues.label: ID photo
clues.finding: Far more than joining a raffle needs. An ID photo is valuable to identity thieves.

clues.label: Privacy notice
clues.finding: Without a notice you can't know why your data is collected or what happens to it (transparency).

clues.label: Free entry
clues.finding: Free raffles are normal. Not a warning sign on its own.

clues.label: Staff
clues.finding: Uniforms are easy to copy and prove little either way. Not a warning sign on its own.

indicators.title: Asks for an ID photo
indicators.whyItMatters: Collect only what is needed (proportionality).

indicators.title: Asks for your birthdate
indicators.whyItMatters: Birthdates help thieves pretend to be you.

indicators.title: No privacy notice
indicators.whyItMatters: People must be told why their data is collected (transparency).

questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.message: A scammer who gets into one account may use it to get into your others. Which account needs the strongest protection?
choices: Your online game account
Your main email account, which receives password-reset links
Your music streaming account
An old forum account you no longer use
questions.explanation: "Forgot password" links go to your email. Whoever controls your email can reset your other accounts: social media, e-wallets and school. Protect it first with a unique password and MFA (a second check, like a code).
questions.feedback: Your email is the master key. Every "Forgot password" link goes there.
questions.hint: Where do "Forgot password" links get sent?
questions.learningObjective: Protect first the account that unlocks all the others.
questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 9: Information Assets and Asset Management ("evaluate their value and protection requirements")

questions.subject: SYSTEM SECURITY ALERT
questions.message: Your computer is INFECTED and LOCKED. Call Certified Support at 1-800-555-0199 now. DO NOT restart your computer.
questions.scenarioContext: While browsing, a full-screen red page appeared and started beeping.
questions.explanation: This is a tech-support scam. Real warnings come from your computer's own security app, not from a web page with a phone number. The "support" person will ask for money or control of your PC. Close the tab. If it's stuck, close the browser with Task Manager.
questions.feedback: Scam! Real alerts come from your computer's settings, never from a web page that tells you to call.
questions.hint: Where do real security warnings come from: a web page, or your own computer?
questions.learningObjective: Know where real security alerts come from.
questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Operating System Security ("patch management, and security configuration")

clues.label: The page
clues.finding: A page you didn't ask for, from a site you don't know.

clues.label: The alert
clues.finding: Big red alerts are designed to cause panic.

clues.label: The claim
clues.finding: A web page can't scan your computer. It's only a page made to scare you.

clues.label: What it wants
clues.finding: Real security warnings never ask you to call a number. This is a tech-support scam.

clues.label: The instruction
clues.finding: It keeps you on the scary page. Closing the browser usually ends it.

indicators.title: Fake infection claim
indicators.whyItMatters: Web pages can't see what's on your computer.

indicators.title: Asks you to call 'support'
indicators.whyItMatters: Real warnings don't come with a phone number.

indicators.title: Keeps you from closing it
indicators.whyItMatters: Pressure is the scam's main tool.

questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.message: You paid ₱1,500 to an online seller through PayLite. The seller then blocked you and never shipped. What should you do first?
choices: Delete the chat so you can move on
Post the seller's photo and threaten them publicly
Send another payment because they say it "unlocks" your refund
Save proof (the chat, the seller's profile and the receipt with its reference number), then report to PayLite and the police
questions.explanation: Proof is what lets PayLite and the police help you, and the reference number can help trace the money. Deleting the chat destroys proof. Public threats can get you in trouble. "Pay more to get a refund" is a second scam.
questions.feedback: Save the proof first: chat, profile and reference number. Then report it.
questions.hint: After a scam, what will the e-wallet company and the police ask you to show them?
questions.learningObjective: Save proof before doing anything else.
questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Digital Evidence and Evidence Collection ("collection, preservation, and documentation")

clues.label: Your chat
clues.finding: The chat shows what was agreed and paid. Keep it - it's evidence.

clues.label: Blocked
clues.finding: Being blocked after paying is a classic sign of a fake seller. Save everything before it disappears.

clues.label: Payment receipt
clues.finding: The reference number lets PayLite trace where the money went.

clues.label: Seller's profile
clues.finding: The seller's account details help the platform and the police find them.

indicators.title: The chat history
indicators.whyItMatters: Proof of what was agreed. Deleting it destroys evidence.

indicators.title: Receipt with reference number
indicators.whyItMatters: Reference numbers can help trace the money.

indicators.title: Seller's account details
indicators.whyItMatters: They let the platform and the police act.

questions.subject: Password reset request
questions.message: We received a request to reset your password. This link expires in 15 minutes. If you didn't request this, you can ignore this email.
questions.scenarioContext: One minute before this email arrived, you clicked "Forgot password" on NovaCloud yourself. Trusted domain (case files): novacloud.example
questions.explanation: You asked for this reset yourself a minute ago. The address matches the trusted one exactly, and it doesn't ask for your password. It even says you can ignore it if you didn't ask. Not every message is a scam!
questions.feedback: Legitimate! You asked for it, the address matches, and it doesn't ask for your password.
questions.hint: Read the case note. Did you ask for this, and does the address match the trusted one?
questions.learningObjective: Real messages exist too: check the facts before calling something a scam.
questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Weeks 7–8: Principles of Information Assurance (authentication)

clues.label: Sender address
clues.finding: no-reply@novacloud.example matches the trusted domain in your case files.

clues.label: Expiry
clues.finding: Short expiry times are normal for reset links - it's a security feature, not pressure.

clues.match: If you didn't request this, you can ignore this email.
clues.label: No pressure
clues.finding: It lets you ignore it if you didn't ask. A scam would push you to act.

clues.label: Reset link
clues.finding: It goes to novacloud.example, the trusted domain - and you asked for this reset a minute ago.

indicators.whyItMatters: Matches novacloud.example in your case files.

indicators.title: Link to the real domain
indicators.whyItMatters: And you requested the reset yourself.

indicators.title: No pressure
indicators.whyItMatters: You can safely ignore it if you didn't ask.

questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.message: A message links to: https://examplebank.example.account-verify.example/login. Which is true?
choices: It's ExampleBank's site because "examplebank" appears first
It's safe because it uses HTTPS
It's a subdomain trick: the real domain is account-verify.example
It's a misspelled (typosquatted) bank domain
questions.explanation: To find the real website, read the address from right to left, up to the first single "/". Here it is account-verify.example. The "examplebank" in front is a decoy the scammer added. Nothing is misspelled, and HTTPS doesn't make it safe.
questions.feedback: Read right to left: the real site is account-verify.example. The bank's name is just a decoy.
questions.hint: Read the web address from right to left, up to the first single slash.
questions.learningObjective: Find the real website in a link by reading right to left.
questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Web and Application Security

clues.label: https://
clues.finding: HTTPS only encrypts the connection. It doesn't tell you who owns the site.

clues.label: The left part
clues.finding: Everything to the left of the real domain is a subdomain - the attacker can write anything there, even a bank's name.

clues.label: The real domain
clues.finding: Read the domain from the right, ending just before the first single '/'. The real domain is account-verify.example.

clues.label: The path
clues.finding: The part after the '/' can say anything. It doesn't change who owns the site.

clues.label: The page
clues.finding: Copying a bank's look is easy. Nothing is misspelled here, so this isn't typosquatting either.

indicators.title: Real domain: account-verify.example
indicators.whyItMatters: The domain decides who owns the page.

indicators.title: Bank name used as a subdomain
indicators.whyItMatters: Subdomain tricks put a trusted name on the left.

questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.message: A login page shows a padlock and starts with https://. What does the padlock actually prove?
choices: The site is owned by the real company
Data between you and this site is encrypted, but the site itself could still be fake
The site has been checked by the government
The site cannot contain malware
questions.explanation: The padlock (HTTPS) means your connection is private, so others can't read what you send. It doesn't say who owns the site. Anyone can get a padlock, scam sites too, so you still need to check the address.
questions.feedback: Padlock = private connection, not safe site. Fake sites have padlocks too.
questions.hint: A padlock is about the connection. Does it tell you who owns the site?
questions.learningObjective: Know that a padlock doesn't mean a site is real.
questions.curriculumRef: Advanced Cybersecurity Strategies (BIT4233). Supporting: Computer Security (BIT1225), Cryptography — Modern Cryptography ("secure data in transit and at rest")

clues.label: https://
clues.finding: The 's' means the connection uses TLS encryption. Others on the network can't read or change your data.

clues.label: The padlock
clues.finding: The connection is private - data in transit is encrypted. It says nothing about who runs the site.

clues.label: The certificate
clues.finding: Certificates are easy for anyone to get for their own domain - scam sites have padlocks too.

clues.label: The form
clues.finding: A padlock doesn't make a form safe to fill in. You still have to check the domain.

indicators.title: Encrypted connection
indicators.whyItMatters: That's what the padlock actually means.

indicators.title: Anyone can get a certificate
indicators.whyItMatters: So a padlock can't prove the site is the real company.

questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.message: SMS from an unknown number: "Ma, si Migs 'to. Nasira phone ko, bagong number ko 'to. Pa-send naman ₱3,000 sa PayLite 0917 555 0188, emergency lang. Wag ka muna tumawag, wala pa akong load." What attack is this? In English: "Mom, it's Migs. My phone broke, this is my new number. Please send ₱3,000 to PayLite 0917 555 0188, it's an emergency. Don't call yet, I have no load."
choices: Impersonation: someone pretending to be family with a "new number"
Malware infection
A data breach
A promotional spam message
questions.explanation: A "family member" with a new number, a sudden emergency, a money request and "don't call me" are classic signs. This trick is called social engineering: it uses your feelings, not hacking. Call Migs's old number, or ask something only he would know.
questions.feedback: Impersonation! New number + emergency + "don't call" = call the old number first.
questions.hint: A new number, an emergency, a money request and "don't call me". How could you check it's really him?
questions.learningObjective: Spot scams that use feelings and rush you, and check through a number you know.
questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Weeks 10–11: Cybersecurity Threats and Attack Landscape

clues.label: Sender
clues.finding: Not in your contacts. The first text explains it away with a 'new number'.

clues.label: "New number"
clues.finding: Claiming to be family on a new number is how impersonators skip your contacts list.

clues.label: The request
clues.finding: The whole story leads to one thing: send money now.

questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.message: A classmate's school account password was stolen through phishing. Which protection would most likely stop the attacker from logging in?

A privacy screen protector
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the account
Clearing the browser history
questions.explanation: MFA (multi-factor authentication) asks for a second check, like a code or an app prompt, as well as the password. So a stolen password alone isn't enough. The other choices don't stop someone logging in from far away. Only approve prompts you started yourself.
questions.feedback: MFA! A stolen password alone isn't enough, as long as you never approve a prompt you didn't start.

Turn off your firewall so the network connects faster

The document is just read-only

questions.message: A friend was scammed through a chat app and wants to file a report. Which way of handling the evidence is best?

Keep the original chat untouched, take full screenshots (with names, dates and times), save receipts, share only copies, and note when you saved each one
Uninstall the app to stop the scammer and write down what you remember

The subject mentions tuition
The display name says "Registrar's Office"
It was sent at 2:14 AM
questions.explanation: The "From" name can say anything. SPF and DMARC are checks that ask: did the school's own mail system really send this? Both failed. Reply-To also sends your answer to the scammer. The subject and the time are only weak clues.
questions.feedback: SPF and DMARC failed, and replies go to free-mail. The "From" name is just text anyone can type.
questions.hint: The "From" name is just text. Which lines are checks the mail system actually ran?
questions.learningObjective: Trust an email's hidden checks, not just what it shows.
questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Network Forensics and Cybercrime Investigation ("identify signs of cybercrimes")

clues.finding: DMARC fail: the email doesn't line up with the registrar's own domain policy.
